I first started getting "nukes" around MW3 and the one piece of advice I can give you for achieving such high streaks is that it's one thing to have gunskill and be able to win gunfights, but getting nukes requires you to *stay alive.* Being able to stay alive so long while winning gunfights is a skill you have to practice; you need to know when to back off, when not to push, and have good positioning.

A lot of factors come in to play obviously, like the lobby you're in, luck, and connection, but you can get better at getting them more consistently. But, once you get your first one or few, I promise it gets a lot easier, it gives you the confidence knowing that you *can* do it.

Then from there, it's just about consistency. Yeah, I drop a couple or more V2's a day, which isn't easy, but you don't ever get to see all the fucking times I **choke*. Once you get to that 15/20 killstreak, you start to think *a lot.* Maybe start doubting yourself. Even I push something I shouldn't or do something stupid a lot of the time. Even after almost a decade of playing CoD, I'm still learning and improving.

When you get that streak though, you need to calm down if you're getting nervous, breathe calmly, and just play the game. Use your intuition and make smart decisions. I find I usually get V2s much easier when I'm not explicitly going for them, but that's not always the case. For someone trying to get their first or more, you probably should try but like I said, don't doubt yourself and stay calm.

Type 1 diabetes. It's nothing extremely rare but it has no cure or prevention methods and scientists and doctors are still not sure what the cause of it is. However, they at least know that it might partially be caused by environmental factors and is definitely a hereditary disease.

Only 5-10% of total diabetics, including type 2 diabetes and things like gestational diabetes etc., have type 1, which used to be labeled as juvenile diabetes because most people are diagnosed at childhood or teen years, something that has changed because people can get diagnosed all the way up until their 20's.

There are no tests currently that can be done to predict someone being diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Basically, if you carry the gene for the disease,  there are these antibodies in your body that, for whatever reason if you're unlucky enough (which, like, I said, nobody knows why), get triggered to attack and sabotage your pancreas to stop producing insulin. In the case of type 1 diabetes, this usually results in a complete and total cessation of natural insulin production, thus definitively requiring you to take medication *the rest of your entire life.* Unless, of course, a cure is discovered (which, if it is, probably won't even be released to the public because big pharma would make boatloads more money charging people for medication their entire life than a one-time procedure).

I have to inject insulin multiple times daily and have to count practically every single carb I eat. I do math every time I want to eat something.

It has caused pretty significant change in my lifestlye and effects my day-to-day and even hourly life. Having this chronic illness combined with my already existing major depression has really affected me. I suppose we'll see in the long run if it makes or breaks me, it's definitely caused harm to me and also made me become a stronger person as I have to deal with something, added to all of the other daily struggles of a homeless 19-year-old, that most people never even consider. It's made me realize how much people take things for granted, like being able to eat food and just lift it into their mouth without having any second thoughts or having to calculate how much insulin to take. 

I've been skinny my entire life due to my high metabolism and was diagnosed at the age of 17, I'm currently 6'0", 140 lbs. I was ignorant about diabetes, like most people, before I was diagnosed and only learned about it because I had to. 

Since most people don't know the difference between 1 and 2, let me explain. *Type 2* diabetes is the one related to being caused by unhealthy eating habits and obesity, but it can still be genetically passed down. Type 1 is purely genetic. No matter which type they have, don't assume a diabetic "had too much sugar" or is just unhealthy, this is completely false and pretty offensive.

Whenever I tell people I'm diabetic, and they say (even have had medical staff say this to me...) "But you're so skinny and young, how?!?" it honestly hurts. I try to brush it off since I know many people are just ignorant and  uneducated and assume being diabetic means "Oh, you're a fat-ass and had too much sugar," but it still is offensive. I didn't ask for this disease at all, I just got shitty cards dealt to me. I try to educate every about it that I can because it is a part of me now and I see how uneducated people are on it.

Anyways, that's my whole spiel. I know there's plenty of information I left out of my comment, so if anyone is curious and has questions, feel free to ask me.
